1.transcript: Transcript: Lanmorick priory. The survey of the eighteen forties first. Its measurements read as the restorers' job order: the bays to be underpinned are dimensioned to the inch, the roof they meant to strip is in section, the untouched north aisle gets one overall length. It records the intended works, and little besides. Marrable argues it was a pupils' exercise whose errors march in the order they worked; the surveyors were the contractor's own men, paid by the day out of the works account. Pennoy tells his students the field books beat the drawings made from them; the books hand the draughtsmen the same tidy figures. It did catch the south range that fell in eighteen fifty-one — in two lines and a width. The scan, now. The tower's cross-section comes out an oval, wider by a foot on the river face. It stands plumb to within a finger's breadth. Someone asked about the top stage: it sits true on the axis of the ones below. And the courses run level, rather than wavering as ground movement would leave them. Next, the roof spaces — the first campaign stopped at the wall heads — go up in the spring. Loading was settled last year by the engineers. Repeatability we tested at the outset, on the chapter house. The parish's other early buildings are a different grant and a different decade. The choir's mason's marks. Three-quarters sit in the two rebuilt bays, so they date the repairs rather than parcelling out the building seasons. The quarry marks are a separate alphabet. And the spacing wanders half a foot inside a single bay.

options.C: Its upper stage sits slightly off the axis of the stages beneath it
options.D: Its courses undulate in a way consistent with ground movement while building was under way

2.transcript: Transcript: The Dunmere wordbook, issued in parts. Lensham reads the prefaces as replies to the reviewers. I part company with her. Beside the subscription lists they are aimed at the people paying: thanks for patience, promises about the next part, apologies for the price. The first preface already names its subscribers, forty of them, before any notice appeared. The passages Lensham matches were in print before the reviews she pairs them with. The staff, meanwhile, got their instructions on printed slips, weekly. The archive is being catalogued. When that is done we shall see how the labour was shared out: each editor marked the material in his own ink, and those marks are on the slips still. Cut entries went with the proofs, and the proofs were pulped. The packets were opened by a clerk who kept the slips and burned the wrappers. The chief editor's annotated rival sits in a private collection in Dunmere. One entry to dwell on: a dialect name for a fishing float. It went to proof, then was pulled and reset — a second pass its neighbours were spared. Its evidence came in from four counties. You will read that its definition survives in six drafts; one draft survives, and a fair copy. Its etymology was wrong, and corrected in the second printing. Last, the slip recount. The collection grew fastest in the very years the annual reports call lean. The boxes for the commonest words are the fattest in the run. For the late letters the published figures run under the true holdings. And the misfiled slips are from the last decade of collecting.

options.A: Its evidence came from a single county, which forced a decision about regional labels
options.B: It was reset in type after the first proof, needing a second pass unlike its neighboring entries
options.C: Its definition survives in six successive drafts, which show the house style taking shape
options.D: An error in its etymology outlived four printings, showing how slowly corrections spread

3.transcript:
Transcript: The measured mile off Aberwynt. In eighteen ninety-four a coal company put a pier across the sight line from the northern beacon, and the course had to be shifted a mile down the coast and surveyed afresh. The navy paid for the beacons and the navy paid to move them. Porthlenny's figures do sit a touch high, but the two grounds were surveyed to one standard and convert cleanly. And the timings came off the ship's own stopwatches, not from the shore huts.

Now, the yard papers, catalogued last winter. What I expect from them is the post survey: how far the marker posts had drifted from the distance the charts gave them. The Penvorran's propellers are in her completion book — the pair she carried into service. Her draught was read off the marks that morning and both sides signed for it. And the sister ship was six months from launching.

Nansveor charges the fleet with inflating trial speeds. I go part way with him. The export figures run high, by a knot and a half, and that was not an error in the current allowance but a decision taken ashore. The home trials come out straight, year after year.

Coal returns, finally. Ships tried in the winter months returned higher figures than those tried in summer. One of you suggested the stokers: sort the returns by stokehold and they scatter less than they do by ship. Trial-day burning sits above what the same ships used on passage. Two yards did return in bushels, and the clerk converted those before the tables were made up.

options.C: The returns were made up in measures that differed from yard to yard and went unreconciled
options.D: Consumption varied more between stokehold crews than between the ships they served in

5.transcript: Transcript: Crown rot, and how far it travels. We ran spore samplers out from infected stands, and by distance it made no sense. Plots a few hundred metres out caught as much as the far ones. One five-kilometre plot out-caught everything inside it. Deverow predicted a peak at middling range; the middling plots caught least of the lot. Sort that catch by collector height and it lines up: tall masts caught heavily wherever they stood. We measured our hardware. Hedravean. Its harvest books run back a hundred and twenty years, and their bad years let us date outbreaks nobody recorded as disease. Managed ground, yes, but nobody has ever counted its trees — no population to calibrate against. Its growers spray about as often as the foresters. And we went to them: six years in before a grower wrote to us. Moving north? Ferrow says the northern records track our new sites. But those northern stands were surveyed clean twice before, and it is in them now. I credit the spread. Hallick reads the records as movement up the river valleys; the new finds sit north of the valleys' heads. The old southern specimens went back under the microscope — they are the same fungus. Next season, the edges. Our collectors have sat well inside the plots. The spore season shuts down by October, so autumn stays our stopping point. The cartridge readers do more, granted, but want mains power; our plots are an hour's walk from the nearest road. A gauge at each collector would be duplication, not data: rain we already log, from the met station beside plot four.

8.transcript:
Transcript: The Trevoggan gorge salamanders — eleven seasons, and what the survey has measured.

Identification first. We have tagged these animals since the start; the tags come out of the budget after this season. What replaces them is a photograph, taken in the hand and matched by software against the spot pattern. Someone asked whether the adults would still be tagged. They won't — the camera treats an adult and a first-year alike.

The recapture figures. Estimates from the spring sessions ran well above the autumn ones for the same reach. We have run the same forty trap-nights a session since the third year, and both ends of the valley rise and fall together. A dozen did reappear within days of release, sooner than the model allows; too few to move the model.

So what have we measured? Mostly ourselves. Three stretches near the road supply the bulk of the detections, and those are the stretches we like walking. Weather counts, I grant you — a warm wet night doubles what enters a trap — but that washes out across a season, and our footpaths do not. Sort the catch by size and the same proportions come back each year. Hanwolla, before me, wrote that the animals shuttle onto the slopes in dry years; the slope transects came back with a handful of animals whatever the weather.

Polgrenna's second breeding site. Eggs turn up in the known pools a fortnight before the first young appear, in wet years and dry ones alike. The young come in one short pulse, ten days and done, and the pulse falls in the low-water weeks.

options.A: Estimates from the spring sessions ran well above the autumn ones for the same reach
options.B: The estimate climbed year on year until the season the trapping effort was cut back
options.C: Figures from the two ends of the valley moved independently of each other
options.D: Animals reappeared far sooner after release than the model said they should

9.transcript:
Transcript: Morgelly's studio ledger — Threlmoor, thirty years of sittings.

Pricing first. Across the square, Ivestead charged one fee for the sitting however many prints went out; Morgelly charged by the print. Ivestead's sitting stood a shilling below Morgelly's, and a group paid that same shilling again. His fee rose twice in twenty years, both times when he took larger premises. One of you had read that he discounted for regulars. His book gives the same figure for a stranger and for a man on his fourth sitting.

Chelvern says the ledger was written up afterwards, for show. I don't accept it. The ink shifts from entry to entry, the way a book kept daily will; the hand is his throughout, which tells us who wrote it, not when. The earliest volume shows the same ink shifts as the later ones. So: not an open question but a settled one — the ink changes at the entry.

Now, the plate makers' price lists. His exposures hold at about the same length right through the change of plates, and his invoices are bound into the back of the same ledger. The interest is not what he bought but what he sold on: the counter trade in plates and chemicals brought him more than the camera work did.

Which leaves the light. The handbook figures reach his pages a good decade after the journals printed them. He opens up a stop for children; past that, the settings answer the sky. It won't date his prints — half the sittings go unnamed — but knowing his habits, it reads as an instrument.

11.transcript: Transcript: Trelundy infirmary and its weighing scheme. The dispenser's ledger first: it is a costing book. Extra diet, coals, the man's own hours, priced week by week; the total ran heavy enough that the governors twice set the scheme down for debate, and twice let it stand. Occupancy you get elsewhere: bed numbers come from the matron's returns. There are marginal notes, granted, haggling over the price of oatmeal. We date the break from the governors' minutes; the ledger runs unbroken through those years. The weighing itself. Physicians read the charts as a record of recovery. The ward staff had quite other ends in view: Friday's figures settled who could be put to work on the ward. The scale came in with a physician in the house's first month, and the kitchen inspections start twenty years later. Someone asked whether the balance was swapped — it was the same beam throughout. And the weighing did fix the shape of the week; true, though it is not my point. Maderwyn re-read the registers. Weight and length of stay track each other far more loosely than the reports of the day claimed. Winter and summer intakes gained at much the same rate. The gains scatter across quarter-ounces. The attendants' books disagree constantly rather than running alike. Rostrellick says the weighing shaped admission. His notes come from the eighteen sixties, a generation after the weighing began. Subscribers nominated, certainly, though the house physician struck names off the nomination lists. Until the admission registers are worked through, our papers cannot settle it — and I am withholding judgment on both ends.

options.D: Its running totals let historians work out how many beds the house actually kept filled

17.transcript:
Transcript: The Marnstow estuary: the silt record, and what we do next.

Here is the claim: the shoaling follows the works along the banks far more closely than anything the river brings down. Each training wall shows in the soundings inside three years of being built, and the mean depth at the bar changed by six feet inside forty years. The board did add stations where it wanted a case, I grant that; drop those stations and the pattern stands.

What next? We core the three reaches the series marks as gaining fastest, to see whether the mud agrees. Not further back into the paper — the older harbour charts can wait. The raw sounding books are already on the shelf at the record office. And the lead line was run beside modern gear in the seventies; they agree to a few inches.

Ordwell's replotting. He expected the deep water to have crept toward the town shore, and said so in his first paper; his replot put it back where the charts had it. What he found instead: after each dredging the channel fills quickest through the first winter, then slackens off. Two stations had moved between crews, and Ordwell renamed them before plotting. The monthly gauge shows shoals sitting put for years at a time.

Why Fenrith? The ferry keeper's own depth notes cover the years the official series leaves blank. The slip was rebuilt at some point — the parish argued for years about which year. The silting suit came sixty years after the gap. And that painting in the town hall: the tide in it is anyone's guess.

21.transcript: Transcript: The Dunmere wordbook, issued in parts. Lensham reads the prefaces as replies to the reviewers. I part company with her. Beside the subscription lists they are aimed at the people paying: thanks for patience, promises about the next part, apologies for the price. The first preface already names its subscribers, forty of them, before any notice appeared. The passages Lensham matches were in print before the reviews she pairs them with. The staff, meanwhile, got their instructions on printed slips, weekly. The archive is being catalogued. When that is done we shall see how the labour was shared out: each editor marked the material in his own ink, and those marks are on the slips still. Cut entries went with the proofs, and the proofs were pulped. The packets were opened by a clerk who kept the slips and burned the wrappers. The chief editor's annotated rival sits in a private collection in Dunmere. One entry to dwell on: a dialect name for a fishing float. It went to proof, then was pulled and reset — a second pass its neighbours were spared. Its evidence came in from four counties. You will read that its definition survives in six drafts; one draft survives, and a fair copy. Its etymology was wrong, and corrected in the second printing. Last, the slip recount. The collection grew fastest in the very years the annual reports call lean. The boxes for the commonest words are the fattest in the run. For the late letters the published figures run under the true holdings. And the misfiled slips are from the last decade of collecting.

23.transcript: Transcript: Lanmorick priory. The survey of the eighteen forties first. Its measurements read as the restorers' job order: the bays to be underpinned are dimensioned to the inch, the roof they meant to strip is in section, the untouched north aisle gets one overall length. It records the intended works, and little besides. Marrable argues it was a pupils' exercise whose errors march in the order they worked; the surveyors were the contractor's own men, paid by the day out of the works account. Pennoy tells his students the field books beat the drawings made from them; the books hand the draughtsmen the same tidy figures. It did catch the south range that fell in eighteen fifty-one — in two lines and a width. The scan, now. The tower's cross-section comes out an oval, wider by a foot on the river face. It stands plumb to within a finger's breadth. Someone asked about the top stage: it sits true on the axis of the ones below. And the courses run level, rather than wavering as ground movement would leave them. Next, the roof spaces — the first campaign stopped at the wall heads — go up in the spring. Loading was settled last year by the engineers. Repeatability we tested at the outset, on the chapter house. The parish's other early buildings are a different grant and a different decade. The choir's mason's marks. Three-quarters sit in the two rebuilt bays, so they date the repairs rather than parcelling out the building seasons. The quarry marks are a separate alphabet. And the spacing wanders half a foot inside a single bay.

Transcript: The Trevoggan gorge salamanders — eleven seasons, and what the survey has measured.

Identification first. We have tagged these animals since the start; the tags come out of the budget after this season. What replaces them is a photograph, taken in the hand and matched by software against the spot pattern. Someone asked whether the adults would still be tagged. They won't — the camera treats an adult and a first-year alike.

The recapture figures. Estimates from the spring sessions ran well above the autumn ones for the same reach. We have run the same forty trap-nights a session since the third year, and both ends of the valley rise and fall together. A dozen did reappear within days of release, sooner than the model allows; too few to move the model.

So what have we measured? Mostly ourselves. Three stretches near the road supply the bulk of the detections, and those are the stretches we like walking. Weather counts, I grant you — a warm wet night doubles what enters a trap — but that washes out across a season, and our footpaths do not. Sort the catch by size and the same proportions come back each year. Hanwolla, before me, wrote that the animals shuttle onto the slopes in dry years; the slope transects came back with a handful of animals whatever the weather.

Polgrenna's second breeding site. Eggs turn up in the known pools a fortnight before the first young appear, in wet years and dry ones alike. The young come in one short pulse, ten days and done, and the pulse falls in the low-water weeks.

26.transcript:
Transcript: The measured mile off Aberwynt. In eighteen ninety-four a coal company put a pier across the sight line from the northern beacon, and the course had to be shifted a mile down the coast and surveyed afresh. The navy paid for the beacons and the navy paid to move them. Porthlenny's figures do sit a touch high, but the two grounds were surveyed to one standard and convert cleanly. And the timings came off the ship's own stopwatches, not from the shore huts.

Now, the yard papers, catalogued last winter. What I expect from them is the post survey: how far the marker posts had drifted from the distance the charts gave them. The Penvorran's propellers are in her completion book — the pair she carried into service. Her draught was read off the marks that morning and both sides signed for it. And the sister ship was six months from launching.

Nansveor charges the fleet with inflating trial speeds. I go part way with him. The export figures run high, by a knot and a half, and that was not an error in the current allowance but a decision taken ashore. The home trials come out straight, year after year.

Coal returns, finally. Ships tried in the winter months returned higher figures than those tried in summer. One of you suggested the stokers: sort the returns by stokehold and they scatter less than they do by ship. Trial-day burning sits above what the same ships used on passage. Two yards did return in bushels, and the clerk converted those before the tables were made up.

options.D: What the builders privately took the ship's draught to be on the morning in question

29.transcript: Transcript: Crown rot, and how far it travels. We ran spore samplers out from infected stands, and by distance it made no sense. Plots a few hundred metres out caught as much as the far ones. One five-kilometre plot out-caught everything inside it. Deverow predicted a peak at middling range; the middling plots caught least of the lot. Sort that catch by collector height and it lines up: tall masts caught heavily wherever they stood. We measured our hardware. Hedravean. Its harvest books run back a hundred and twenty years, and their bad years let us date outbreaks nobody recorded as disease. Managed ground, yes, but nobody has ever counted its trees — no population to calibrate against. Its growers spray about as often as the foresters. And we went to them: six years in before a grower wrote to us. Moving north? Ferrow says the northern records track our new sites. But those northern stands were surveyed clean twice before, and it is in them now. I credit the spread. Hallick reads the records as movement up the river valleys; the new finds sit north of the valleys' heads. The old southern specimens went back under the microscope — they are the same fungus. Next season, the edges. Our collectors have sat well inside the plots. The spore season shuts down by October, so autumn stays our stopping point. The cartridge readers do more, granted, but want mains power; our plots are an hour's walk from the nearest road. A gauge at each collector would be duplication, not data: rain we already log, from the met station beside plot four.

options.C: Replace the sticky slides with a filter cartridge that a machine can read
options.D: Set a rain gauge beside each collector so catches can be read against the weather
